## Purpose

This document builds a descriptive BMI summary by income group and gender in R, 
then checks it against a Python/pandas translation in `translation.ipynb`.

## Load the data

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
```

The data path is relative to the repository root. This works at render because `_quarto.yml` sets `execute-dir: project`.

```{r}
#| label: load-data
nhanes <- read_csv(
  "examples/nhanes-equity/data/nhanes_equity_v6.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
```

## Raw data checks

These match the inspection steps in the Python notebook and will inform `parity-table.csv`.

```{r}
#| label: raw-checks
nrow(nhanes)
ncol(nhanes)
names(nhanes)
sum(is.na(nhanes$BMI))
```

## Part A: R Pipeline

```{r}
#| label: part-a-pipeline
r_summary <- nhanes |>
  filter(!is.na(BMI), !is.na(IncomeGroup), !is.na(Gender)) |>
  group_by(IncomeGroup, Gender) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_bmi = round(mean(BMI), 2),
    sd_bmi = round(sd(BMI), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(IncomeGroup, Gender)

r_summary
```

Checks for the parity table: rows left after the missingness filter, the number of grouped rows, and the stored rounded values. 
The table above prints only three significant digits, so the last two lines show the full two-decimal values.

```{r}
#| label: part-a-checks
nrow(filter(nhanes, !is.na(BMI), !is.na(IncomeGroup), !is.na(Gender)))
nrow(r_summary)
r_summary$mean_bmi
r_summary$sd_bmi
```

## Part B: R function

The function wraps the Part A logic so the value and grouping columns are easy to change.

```{r}
#| label: part-b-function
summarise_mean_sd <- function(data, value, group1, group2) {
  data |>
    filter(!is.na({{ value }}), !is.na({{ group1 }}), !is.na({{ group2 }})) |>
    group_by({{ group1 }}, {{ group2 }}) |>
    summarise(
      n = n(),
      mean_value = round(mean({{ value }}), 2),
      sd_value = round(sd({{ value }}), 2),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    arrange({{ group1 }}, {{ group2 }})
}

r_function_summary <- summarise_mean_sd(nhanes, BMI, IncomeGroup, Gender)
r_function_summary
```

Check that the function reproduces the pipeline: same number of rows, same group labels and same rounded values.

```{r}
#| label: part-b-check
nrow(r_function_summary) == nrow(r_summary)
identical(r_function_summary$IncomeGroup, r_summary$IncomeGroup)
identical(r_function_summary$Gender, r_summary$Gender)
identical(r_function_summary$mean_value, r_summary$mean_bmi)
identical(r_function_summary$sd_value, r_summary$sd_bmi)
```

All five checks return `TRUE`, so the function reproduces the pipeline.

## R mastery exercises

### Exercise 1: swap the value column

```{r}
#| label: exercise-1-waist
summarise_mean_sd(nhanes, Waist, IncomeGroup, Gender)
```

**Question:** Check that the grouping labels match the BMI summary. Did the row count change? Why might it?

**Answer:** The group labels match the BMI summary, and there are still 6 grouped rows. The count in each group 
is smaller, though (e.g., 11,397 high-income women instead of 11,743). This is because the function now drops rows 
missing a waist measurement instead of rows missing BMI, so a slightly different set of people is counted.

### Exercise 2: swap a grouping column

```{r}
#| label: exercise-2-race
summarise_mean_sd(nhanes, BMI, Race, Gender)
```

**Question:** How many grouped rows do you get now, and why?

**Answer:** This gives 10 grouped rows: 5 race groups by 2 genders. Together these groups also cover more people 
than the BMI summary. Income group is no longer a grouping column, so rows with missing income are no longer dropped.

## Parity check

The table below is read from `parity-table.csv`. It compares the R results in this document with the Python results in `translation.ipynb`.

```{r}
#| label: parity-table
read_csv(
  "assignments/assignment04-polyglot/submission/parity-table.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

R and Python agree on every check in the table. The only difference is display: the R tibble prints 3 significant digits and drops 
trailing zeros (25.7, 8.2), while pandas shows 25.74 and 8.20; the stored values are the same.

## How to render

From the repository root, run:

```bash
quarto render assignments/assignment04-polyglot/submission/polyglot-parity.qmd
```

This writes `polyglot-parity.html` next to this file. To rerun the Python side, open `translation.ipynb` in the same folder, then 
click Restart and Run All. The notebook calls `helpers.py`, which must stay in the same folder.
